title: 3-Read Friday #24: Misconception Analysis, Belonging, and Matching Technique to Purpose
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 24 centers on assessment, participation, and CPD design. Barton's first pick is the No More Marking/Axiom Maths project analysing distractor patterns in a multiple-choice assessment built from Eedi's own diagnostic question bank, and he flags particular interest in how the specific wrong answer a student chooses correlates with their overall achievement level, promising to follow the study's future instalments. His second selection, Jo Castelino's "Belonging," is framed through Barton's own established enthusiasm for Call and Respond as a participation technique, crediting Castelino with surfacing a benefit - a shared sense of belonging - that he hadn't previously connected to the technique despite using it himself. His third pick, David Didau's piece on matching technique to purpose, gets distilled into a portable CPD principle: training sessions should be built around the underlying purpose a technique serves rather than around the technique itself, since a tool like a mini-whiteboard is only ever a means to that end. The issue's three items cohere loosely around a shared interest in what specific classroom techniques are actually accomplishing beneath their surface mechanics.
points: Barton highlights the No More Marking/Axiom Maths distractor-analysis project as personally significant since it uses his own bank of diagnostic questions, and flags anticipation for further instalments.

His framing of Jo Castelino's belonging piece links it to his own recurring interest in Call and Respond as a participation technique, treating her belonging angle as a genuinely new benefit he hadn't previously articulated.

He distills David Didau's technique-versus-purpose argument into a generalizable CPD principle: sessions should be organized around the purpose being served, not around a named technique like mini-whiteboards.

All three picks this issue orbit around assessment and technique fidelity - how wrong answers reveal misconceptions, how a technique builds belonging, and how technique should follow purpose rather than the reverse.
quotes: The teams at No More Marking and Axiom Maths have taken some of Eedi’s diagnostic multiple-choice questions, given them to nearly 2000 students, and analysed the results.
What I find particularly interesting is how the choice of the wrong answer seems to be influenced by the achievement level of the student.
I like it because it is quick, fun and involves every student. In this fantastic post, Jo points out another benefit - how Call and Respond can engender a sense of belonging in a class.
David makes a really important point that is relevant for anyone delivering CPD, or indeed anyone hoping to bring about a change.

The focus should not be on the technique, but on the purpose. Hence, the session should not be about how to use a mini-whiteboard effectively, but instead how to sustain students’ attention for which the mini-whiteboard can be a useful tool.
